nettle.origin: Textile nettle is chiefly the stinging nettle Urtica dioica (Urticaceae), a perennial with low fertilizer and pesticide needs that grows across most European climate zones. Fiber cultivation relies on selected clones, such as those descended from German breeding collections, rather than wild stands, because selected clones can contain about three times more fiber. Related plants in the same family, including a Himalayan species whose fiber is called allo in western Nepal, supply separate craft traditions. Production is small-scale and experimental.
nettle.structure: Nettle fiber comes from primary bast (phloem) fibers in the stem cortex. In a cultivated German fiber clone, mean fiber diameters were about 19, 32 and 47 microns in the top, middle and bottom of the stem, with average lengths of about 58, 50 and 43 mm, so elementary fibers are long for a bast fiber. Wall thickness ranges from about 1 to over 20 microns. A literature compilation gives roughly 54 percent cellulose, 10 percent hemicellulose, 4 percent pectin, 9 percent lignin, 4 percent wax and fat and 18 percent water-soluble matter, varying with retting and harvest date.
nettle.process: Historical lines resembled hemp processing: stems were dried, defoliated and retted (water retting, or chemical retting with ammonia solution in the First World War period), then broken, scutched to remove woody shives, cooked and hackled. Wartime German research added an unretted flock bast route and the so-called Elster procedure. A current industrial line described for textile-grade nettle harvests cultivated clones mechanically, field-rets and dries the stems, and decorticates them in a hammermill before the fiber is refined for spinning. In western Nepal, allo bark is still stripped by hand, cooked with ash and beaten.
nettle.performance: Nettle behaves like other cellulosic bast fibers: strong and relatively stiff when dry, with good moisture absorption and a cool, linen-like hand when finely processed. Fine, long elementary fibers allow smoother yarns than hemp, but quality depends heavily on clone, stem position, retting and the degree of degumming. It takes direct, reactive and vat dyes. Like flax, it creases, and residual lignin can yellow in light. Leaves and stinging hairs are removed early in processing.
nettle.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: nettle burns like linen, with a paper-like smell and gray ash. Microscopy shows long bast cells with visible lumens and cross-markings similar to flax and ramie, so nettle is easily confused with those fibers. Archaeological studies have combined fiber microscopy with provenance analysis to infer where the plants grew. Products sold as nettle are often blends or actually ramie (Boehmeria nivea, also Urticaceae), so fiber-content testing is advisable.
nettle.labeling: Nettle is not among the Annex I fibre names of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Under that regulation, fibres not yet listed may be designated as other fibres with their percentage, and a label such as 100% other fibres (nettle) has been described as an acceptable approach. In the US, textile products covered by the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act and 16 CFR Part 303 must disclose fiber content, and natural fibers are named by common name. Ramie must not be labeled as nettle simply because both are in the nettle family.
nettle.past: Nettle textiles are ancient in Europe: the roughly 2,800-year-old Lusehoj Bronze Age textile from Voldtofte, Denmark, has been identified as nettle, probably imported from the region of present-day Carinthia and Styria in Austria. During the First World War Germany expanded nettle fiber production when flax and cotton stocks ran out, using fabric for army uniforms and paying schoolchildren to collect stems. Gustav Bredemann began systematic clone selection in the 1920s, research revived in the Second World War, and interest waned after 1945 until renewed breeding and processing trials from the 1990s.

banana.origin: Banana fiber is taken from the leaf sheaths that make up the pseudostem of cultivated Musa species and cultivars, most of them triploid descendants of Musa acuminata and Musa balbisiana. Leading banana producers include India, China, Indonesia, Brazil, Ecuador and the Philippines. Because a large share of banana plant biomass is left as residue after the bunch is harvested, pseudostem fiber is promoted as a waste-derived material. Okinawa's bashofu cloth uses a specific plant, Musa balbisiana var. liukiuensis.
banana.structure: The pseudostem is built of concentric leaf sheaths. Fibers from the outer sheaths are coarser, with diameters approaching 250 microns, while inner sheaths yield finer fibers near 50 to 100 microns; overall banana fiber diameters are reported at about 56 to 350 microns. Cellulose content is intermediate, below 70 percent in reported banana and plantain samples, with moderate lignin. The fibers contain microvoids, and apparent density is reported at about 0.65 to 1.5 g/cm3. Bashofu artisans select sheaths whose fibers have thin cell walls and smooth, white surfaces.
banana.process: After the bunch is cut, the pseudostem must be processed quickly because its high water content invites decay. Sheaths are separated with a knife, and fiber is extracted mainly from the outer and intermediate sheaths, since the innermost layers resist abrasion poorly. Extraction may be manual scraping, a mobile-blade decorticator in which the sheath is pulled between pressing knives (small units handle roughly 10 to 20 kg of fiber per day), or larger mechanical extractors. Fiber is washed, dried and, for textiles, softened and often cottonized or blended. In bashofu production, fibers are cleaned by hand (u-biki) and spooled (u-umi) as they are joined into continuous yarn.
banana.performance: Banana fiber is strong but stiff and relatively inextensible, with a hand that ranges from crisp and papery in traditional handwoven cloth to soft in cottonized blends. It is hydrophilic and swells when wet; alkali treatment removes surface impurities and improves adhesion in composites. Thermal stability is limited, to roughly 230 C before significant degradation. It takes direct and reactive dyes. Its variability in diameter and aspect ratio, caused by sheath position, is the main obstacle to consistent spinning.
banana.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: banana fiber burns like other cellulosics. Microscopy shows bundles of lumened cells similar to abaca. Because abaca is also a Musa species, microscopy and FTIR cannot reliably separate banana fiber from abaca, and trade names should not be treated as proof of species. Many banana-fiber garments are blends with cotton or regenerated cellulose, so fiber-content testing is needed to verify percentages.
banana.labeling: Banana fiber has no separate Annex I name in Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011; abaca (Musa textilis) is listed, but using that name for other Musa fibers would misstate the species. Unlisted fibres can be declared as other fibres with their percentage. In the US, covered textiles must disclose fiber content under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act (15 U.S.C. 70 et seq.) and 16 CFR Part 303, naming natural fibers by common name. Claims about agricultural waste origin should be supported by supplier traceability.
banana.past: Banana-family fiber weaving has deep regional roots. In the Ryukyu Islands, bashofu weaving survived in the village of Ogimi in northern Okinawa after nearly disappearing elsewhere in the archipelago, carried on largely by middle-aged and older women who perform the labor-intensive fiber cleaning and spooling stages. Recent scientific work at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology has studied why artisans' traditional fiber selection works. Elsewhere, interest since the 2000s has focused on converting pseudostem waste into textiles, paper and composites.
